title: Musicians and the civil rights movement
summary: Musicians sometimes talked about Little Rock and the sit-ins; Stewart says he was too wrapped up in music to think much about it.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Politics, race and the state of the country

blocks.x: Yeah, right. Now, okay, you -- so now from about 19 -- so from after you left Rose Murphy in around 1959, 1960 or so --

Oh, I know what I wanted to ask you. Like when the civil rights movement began in the 19 -- the mid-'50s, were the musicians talking much about that -- I mean when people began to start -- when Little Rock began and students
began to do the sit-ins and stuff, how did the -- did the musicians talk much about that?

Well, you could hear, once in a while, conversations about that situation, yes. That was more or less a turning point in, what do you call it? Getting together, segregation being -- getting further back in the background, you know, what have you.
How did you feel about that? Did you feel -- how did you feel about those kids who were going out there, trying to change stuff?
Oh, well, I didn't think about it that much, you know. You know, like a lot of those situations, I was so wrapped up in my music, I just didn't bother to think about it too much.
